item.title: Global Development’s Missing Ingredient
item.description: Facing a democracy deficit worldwide, millions of vulnerable people lack avenues through which they can collectively negotiate their interests. Faith-based institutions committed to human dignity and pluralism can play an instrumental role in building the infrastructure required for grassroots organizing at scale.

item.title: China’s External Surplus Makes a “Mandarin Accord” Inevitable
item.description: As with the Plaza Accord in 1985, when the United States and its major trading partners agreed to coordinate policies to weaken the US dollar, an agreement to address global imbalances emanating from China has become increasingly necessary. Given China’s undervalued currency, the situation simply cannot be sustained indefinitely.

item.title: War and Climate
item.description: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz showed how quickly a regional conflict can throw global energy markets into chaos. By pushing governments toward coal and biofuels, the war could accelerate deforestation and undermine climate negotiations, with environmental consequences that will linger long after the fighting ends.

item.title: 9/11’s Long Shadow
item.description: As tragic as the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, were, it was America’s response that truly changed the world. While it is difficult to pinpoint precisely which developments over the last 25 years were caused or compounded by 9/11, it seems clear that the event led the United States to abandon the principles that, with the Cold War over, were supposed to shape a better future.

item.title: The False Politics of Western Declinism
item.description: Political leaders on both sides of the Atlantic increasingly portray the West as being in decline, even as their societies grow richer. By conflating a loss of relative economic power with falling living standards, they give populists an opening to turn domestic grievances into nationalist resentment.

item.title: What 9/11 Did to Us
item.description: For Americans who are old enough to remember them, the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks raised fundamental questions: Who could have done this, and above all, why? We now know that the answers would reshape the country and its place in the world—and not for the better.

item.title: After the AI Bubble Bursts
item.description: Just as debt markets fueled the global financial near-meltdown that followed the 2007–08 subprime-mortgage crisis, their exposure to AI will drive developments now. The problem is that we possess only very limited public information about those markets, and regulators are not making that information any easier to obtain.

item.title: Trump Is Stoking Territorial Revisionism
item.description: Donald Trump’s refusal to respect international borders has already led Argentina and Morocco to revive territorial disputes and has effectively given Israel carte blanche to operate where it sees fit. But this might be just the beginning: if the US can claim land and resources on the basis of vague national-security claims, anyone can.

item.title: Have the Terrorists Won?
item.description: The point of terrorism is not to cause suffering, but to provoke the target into doing something that hurts it even more. In the quarter-century since the 9/11 attacks, the US has done just that, leaving the world and itself worse off.

item.title: How 9/11 Fractured the Global Order
item.description: The terrorist attack on the United States 25 years ago remains among the most consequential events of this century. By fundamentally altering the trajectories of the United States and Russia, as well as that of a rising China, al-Qaeda’s attack set in motion developments that would produce the geopolitical tumult we live in today.

item.title: China’s Permanent Manufacturing Revolution
item.description: In developed economies, manufacturing employment will decline, regardless of industrial strategies pursued. China's competitiveness means that any expectation that manufacturing will absorb more than a trivial fraction of the large increases in the working-age population still occurring in India or Africa is a delusion.

item.title: Europe Needs Dual-Use Defense Spending
item.description: Some EU countries, such as Poland, are using their expanded defense budgets to buy more foreign hardware. A better approach would be to foster a thriving innovation ecosystem which ensures that the technologies, institutions, and people that underpin a strong military benefit the civilian economy as well.

item.title: The World 9/11 Didn’t Make
item.description: Looking back at the past quarter-century, it becomes apparent that the 9/11 terrorist attack against the United States was not a transformative event. Far more important developments have intervened, not least America’s rejection of the postwar order that it had a large hand in building.

item.title: The BRICS at 20
item.description: If the promise of the BRICS was to establish a monetary union, a single market, or a tightly integrated political alliance, it has not been fulfilled. But if it was to build a platform for emerging economies to cooperate while advancing their own strategic autonomy, the BRICS has exceeded expectations.

item.title: Europe’s Security Depends on a Clear Electrification Target
item.description: The politics around electrification are beginning to shift in Europe as more people recognize its importance for economic competitiveness and industrial resilience. European Union policymakers should seize this momentum to embed a binding target of at least 50% electrification by 2040 in the bloc’s energy security framework.

item.title: The AI Race Could Sink US-China Détente
item.description: The competition between the United States and China to develop AI and deploy it globally poses the biggest threat to the two countries’ currently constructive relations. Without an ongoing AI dialogue to avoid escalation, a return to the zero-sum conflict that rattled both sides last year cannot be ruled out.

item.title: Are China’s Rare Earths Really a Potent Weapon?
item.description: The available evidence indicates that Chinese rare-earth export restrictions would cost the West far less than often feared, though this cost is impossible to estimate precisely in advance. This is forcing prudence on both sides, to the disappointment of geopolitical hawks and the benefit of the global economy.

item.title: The Trump Shock in East Asia
item.description: US President Donald Trump has alarmed his East Asian allies by canceling two joint military exercises with South Korea, a move that seems motivated less by whim than by a fondness for tyrants. The question now is whether South Korea and Japan will set aside historical resentments for the sake of mutual interests.

item.title: Building a Resilient Nepal
item.description: After Japan’s 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, the Japanese government changed the building codes for schools and housing and rethought the placement of critical infrastructure. Nepal (and other vulnerable countries) must pursue a similar approach.
